fields.definition: The specific situation you want to change, described from the point of view of the people affected. A good problem statement says who is affected, where, how much, and why it happens. It does not mention your organisation or what you plan to do.
fields.strongExample: In a rural district, nearly 4 in 10 girls who start secondary school leave before finishing lower secondary, compared with 2 in 10 boys. Families point to the cost of fees, uniforms and transport. Girls describe the long walk to school as unsafe, and many take on more household work as they get older.

weakExample.text: There is a lack of scholarships for girls in our area.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: This describes a missing solution, not the problem. It assumes scholarships are the answer before looking at why girls leave school, and it says nothing about who is affected or how many.
weakExample.improved: Girls in our district leave secondary school earlier than boys. Cost is one of several reasons families give, alongside safety and household work.

fields.tip: Keep it to one or two sentences and narrow it down to a group, a place or one part of a bigger issue. Asking 'why does this happen?' several times helps you move from symptoms to causes, but check your answers against data and against what the people affected tell you. Common explanations don't always hold in every place.

fields.definition: The main things your team will do, using your staff, money and materials, to produce your outputs. Activities are actions, so they start with a verb such as pay, train, run or organise. Describe them specifically enough that someone could plan and budget them.
fields.strongExample: Each year, pay the full secondary school fees for 300 girls who have a place but can't afford to take it, selected with schools using a clear, published rule. Give a bicycle to every girl in the programme who lives more than 3 km from school. Run monthly family groups, led by trained facilitators from the community with village chiefs and religious leaders taking part, on why girls' schooling matters and how household work can be shared.

weakExample.text: Support girls' education in the district.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: This names a cause you care about, not something your team does. It's too vague to plan, cost or check: nobody could tell what happens on a Monday morning.
weakExample.improved: Pay secondary school fees directly to schools for 300 girls each year, and give bicycles to girls who live far from school.

fields.tip: Choose activities that answer the causes in your problem statement. If families name cost and distance, your activities should tackle cost and distance. Keep to the main activities, since the detailed tasks belong in your workplan, and check that each one leads to at least one output. How well an activity is run matters as much as what it is. The same girls' club model that worked well in Uganda failed in Tanzania, where mentors had less training and supervision.

fields.definition: The direct, tangible results of your activities: the products, services or training your project delivers. You can count them, and they are largely within your control. Outputs are what you deliver. Outcomes are the changes that follow in people's lives.
fields.strongExample: Each year, the full fees of 300 girls are paid directly to their schools before term starts, and 180 girls who live more than 3 km away receive a bicycle.

weakExample.text: Girls stay in school and feel safer on the way there.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: These are changes in girls' lives, so they are outcomes. Your project can't deliver them directly, because they depend on the girls, their families and their schools.
weakExample.improved: 180 girls who live more than 3 km from school receive a bicycle at the start of the school year.

fields.tip: Ask of each output: can we deliver and count this ourselves? If the answer depends on other people changing what they do, it's probably an outcome. Words like 'improved', 'increased' or 'strengthened' usually signal an outcome.

fields.definition: The first changes you expect among the people you reach, as a direct result of your outputs. These are usually changes in knowledge, skills, confidence or behaviour. Your project influences them strongly, but doesn't fully control them.
fields.strongExample: Within the first year, girls in the programme attend at least 8 in 10 school days, and more of them move up to the next year group than before.

weakExample.whatIsWrong: This is something the project delivers, so it's an output. It says nothing about what changes for the girls once their fees are paid.
weakExample.improved: Within the first year, more girls in the programme attend school regularly and move up to the next year group.

fields.tip: Write who changes and what changes, for example 'more girls attend school regularly'. If you can't imagine how you'd observe or measure the change, make it more concrete.

The impact of cash transfers on the educational attainment, sexual behavior, and HIV status of adolescent girls in Malawi
sources.organisation: J-PAL (Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab)

fields.definition: Changes that build on the first ones and take longer to appear, often towards the end of the project or soon after. They are usually lasting changes in people's education, health, income or opportunities. Your project contributes to them, alongside other factors.
fields.strongExample: By the end of the project, more girls in the programme finish secondary school than similar girls who weren't in it, and fewer have married or had a child before the age of 18.

weakExample.whatIsWrong: It doesn't say which girls, what changes, compared with what, or by when, so nobody could check whether it happened.
weakExample.improved: By the end of the project, more girls in the programme finish secondary school than similar girls who weren't in it.

fields.tip: The step from short-term to medium-term outcomes is where many theories of change are weakest. Spell out why the first change should lead to the next, and what else must be true. Ask whether the change will last once your support ends. In one evaluation in Malawi, cash payments to girls that weren't tied to school delayed marriage and pregnancy while they lasted, but those effects faded after the payments stopped.

fields.definition: The lasting, long-term change you want to see for the people or place you care about. It usually takes years, goes beyond the life of your project, and depends on many actors. Your project contributes to it, but can't achieve it alone.
fields.strongExample: Young women in the district finish secondary school at the same rate as young men, and have the same chances of going on to further study or paid work.

weakExample.text: End gender inequality in education worldwide.
weakExample.whatIsWrong: It's far beyond what one project can meaningfully contribute to, so it can't guide your choices or show how your work adds up. Nobody could trace your contribution to it.
weakExample.improved: Girls and boys in the district finish secondary school at the same rate.

fields.tip: Many teams start here and work backwards: ask what must already be true just before this change happens, then what must be true before that. Benefits can reach further than you plan. In a long-running study in Ghana, girls given secondary school scholarships later earned more, and their own children were healthier. Name the impact you can credibly contribute to, and mention wider benefits as a hope rather than a promise.
